column1: # What the retired server's durable command queue keeps and what it sweeps,
# the old backlog. Earlier research has the command lifecycle and says
# nothing about retention, the cleanup interval or the sweep at startup.
# Columns: case, subject, value, outcome. A subject of status:X is a command in
# that state. A subject of error:X is the reason a recovered command carries.
# Any other subject is a key in config/config.yaml and the value is what that
# file declares.
# Read from a run, not from the source. Six commands were written straight into
# ./data/commands.db at the ages below, then the server was started with
# queue.cleanup_interval shortened to 3s so the retention sweep could be watched
# inside one session. The binary was built with CGO_ENABLED=1 inside golang:1.26
# on 2026-08-29. The log named `recovered: 1` at startup and `Cleaned up old
# commands, count: 1` three seconds later, and the table then held five rows.
# What the run found:
#   A sent command past queue.recovery_timeout becomes failed, not timeout. The
#   comment beside that key in config/config.yaml says "will be marked as
#   timeout" and CommandStatusTimeout is declared and never assigned.
#   Retention deletes completed commands and nothing else. A pending or failed
#   command is kept at any age, so the file grows without bound for every
#   command that never completed.
#   The recovery sweep runs once, at startup. A sent command inside the window
#   at that moment is never looked at again by it.
#   The core has no durable queue, so an upgrade leaves ./data/commands.db on
#   disk and reads none of it. docs/CHANGELOG.md carries that loss.
